Helga watches from the back; Siggi is beside Óli. Bjarni and Sólveig are among the people. Snow outside is visible at the doorway. No officiating priest, no lettering or legible text, no modern objects. Match the frozen church-meeting scene; do not imply Helga signs.

words_with_history.title: Orð með sögu
text: Á heiðinni leitaði Siggi að bæ Jóns, og Bjarni sagði: „Vestur á heiðinni.“ Svo fór hrafninn vestur á heiðina.
Nú sagði Óli: „Vesturheimur. Það er gott orð.“ Ásta spurði: „Hvað er Vesturheimur?“
Óli sagði: „Ameríka. Þar er land fyrir alla, og vinnumaður er frjáls.“
Afi sagði: „Vestur fer sólin á kvöldin.“
Um nóttina las Helga bækling hjá lampanum. Á honum stóð: Vesturheimur. Siggi sá orðið.
words_with_history.note_en: Vestur + heimur: “the western world”. [?] Vesturheimur was the usual nineteenth-century Icelandic term for America; emigrants were later called vesturfarar (Kafli 20). The chapter shows the characters’ uses without resolving afi’s image.

pronunciation_note.rule: In bauð, au is [øy]; in beit, ei is [ei]; in bárum, á is [au]. In bjóða, jó begins with a j-glide followed by ó. Keep í/i distinct in bíta/bitum, and á/a in bárum/bar. Bitum and bar are pronunciation reference forms, not exercise targets.

grammar.note_en:
A strong past uses an internal stem change instead of the dental suffix ð/d/t of a weak past. Ablaut means this inherited vowel alternation. A class groups verbs with related vowel patterns; it helps predict their parts, but does not replace learning each verb’s principal parts. Compare strong leit, “looked”, with weak horfði, “looked”; both occur here. The table numbers identify the seven traditional strong-verb classes. They are reference labels, not Icelandic number practice.

Dictionary reference only — the five parts are (1) infinitive, the naming form; (2) present third-person singular, “he/she/it …”; (3) past first/third-person singular, “I/he/she/it …”; (4) past first-person plural, “we …”; (5) supine, for later (G21). The fifth form is only a dictionary reference here: it is not a tense by itself and is never an exercise answer. Bíta – bítur – beit – bitum – bitið means “to bite – bites – bit – we bit – supine”; bjóða – býður – bauð – buðum – boðið, “to offer – offers – offered – we offered – supine”; binda – bindur – batt – bundum – bundið, “to bind – binds – bound – we bound – supine”; líta – lítur – leit – litum – litið, “to look – looks – looked – we looked – supine”; svíkja – svíkur – sveik – svikum – svikið, “to betray – betrays – betrayed – we betrayed – supine”. Some reference cells have not appeared in the story. Use the story-attested cells in the tables and exercises; do not practise the unencountered reference cells yet.

The usual four vowel positions are infinitive, singular past, plural past and supine. Class 1: í – ei – i – i, as in bíta and líta. Class 2: jó/jú – au – u – o, as in bjóða. Class 3: for binda, i – a – u – u (other members vary, some with o in the last part); batt also changes the consonants. Class 4: e – a – á – o, as in bera, “carry”. Class 5: e/i – a – á – e, as in gefa, “give”; sitja, “sit”, and liggja, “lie”, are further members, with changes within the stems. Class 6 commonly has a – ó – ó – a/e; hlæja, “laugh”, taka, “take”, and grafa, “dig”, belong here, with hlæja showing a modified present stem. Class 7 descends from verbs with reduplication (a repeated stem element); modern forms are less uniform, often with é or ó in the past. Here hélt, “held”, lét, “put”, and hét, “was called”, have é. These are related patterns, not seven rules that generate every spelling mechanically.

Read the actual cells: beit (s081), “bit”; leit (s042/s046/s059/s119/s124), “looked”; litu (s021), “looked” with a plural subject. Bauð (s084), “offered”, has a singular subject, while buðu (s065/s070/s084), “offered”, has a plural subject. Batt (s077) and bundu (s076/s084) mean “bound”, singular and plural. Bárum (s097) means “we carried”; the same segment’s present ber means “carries”. Gaf (s049/s063) is “gave”; sat (s082/s092/s114), “sat”; lágu (s007), “lay” with a plural subject, and lá (s031), “lay” with a singular subject. Hló (s053/s080) and hlógu (s015/s080) mean “laughed”, singular and plural; tók (s050), “took”; grófu (s025), “dug”; hélt (s055), “held”, and (s079), “held firm”; lét (s050), “put”; hét (s062/s069), “was called”. These cells are listed because this story supplies them; the table does not complete paradigms with unseen forms.

The rule quotes mean: “The wolf bit Týr’s hand off” (s081); “The gods offered the wolf a game” (s084); “Did he bind the wolf too?” (s077, Ásta’s question about Týr, answered no); “I intend to go west too” (s040). Offering and binding are different verbs and classes: bjóða → bauð/buðu versus binda → batt/bundu. The weak pasts talaði, “talked”, skrifaði, “wrote”, and lokaði, “closed”, keep a dental suffix. Bjarni’s comparison is his own; Helga immediately rejects it. The grammar does not explain the myth’s meaning.

Ætla að + infinitive expresses intention: the finite form changes with the subject, while að and the infinitive remain together. Ég ætla, “I intend”, contrasts with þið ætlið, “you (plural) intend”. Ég ætla að fara vestur líka (s040) is “I intend to go west too”; Þið ætlið að svíkja mig (s071), “You intend to betray me”; Í sumar ætla ég að fara með þeim (s100), “This summer I intend to go with them”; Pabbi, ég ætla ekki að fara til Ameríku (s108), “Dad, I do not intend to go to America”. In the last example ekki negates the intention. Hvað ætlar þú að gera á morgun? in C means “What do you intend to do tomorrow?”; the productive present system supplies ætlar. No intention is attributed to Helga.

Keep supported reading items whole. Sem (s009), “who”, adds information about the man. Fleiri en hundrað manns (s018) is “more than a hundred people”; þúsund bændur (s012), “a thousand farmers”. These numerals are supported, never drilled. Eins og Hansen (s006) is “like Hansen”; fínn eins og hár (s069), “fine as hair”. Ef þú skrifar nafnið hér (s033), “if you write your name here”, and ef einhver ykkar leggur hönd í munninn á mér (s072), “if one of you puts a hand in my mouth”, use ef with the indicative, the ordinary statement form of the verb; no conditional paradigm is taught. Kvöldið eftir (s091) means “the following evening”; á kvöldin (s096), “in the evenings”; í ár, “this year”; í sumar, “this summer”. Kann (s060), “know [the story]”, and vill (s056/s058), “wants”, are the G08 items. No perfect, participle construction or middle voice is introduced.
